newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian fishermen's blockade of U.S. ferry grows.
newsitem.headline: Canadian fishermen's blockade of U.S. ferry grows.

text.p: Angrily defying a court order, more Canadian fishermen joined the blockade of an Alaska ferry on Monday as tensions rose between the United States and Canada over salmon fishing.
About 142 passengers were stranded aboard the ferry, which has been prevented from leaving since Saturday. Some 158 others left the ship over the weekend, making alternative travel plans.

About 300 fishing boats -- double the number early in the day -- surrounded the Alaska state ferry Malaspina by Monday afternoon in the harbour at Prince Rupert, British Columbia, 1,000 miles (1,600 km) north of Vancouver.
"The blockade is growing," Jim Sinclair, an official with the United Fishermen and Allied Workers union in Prince Rupert. "People are very upset."
Canada accused the United States of overfishing Pacific Ocean salmon while U.S. officials contended Canada was to blame for scuttling recent talks on a deal to divide this year's catch.
Frustration mounted in British Columbia fishing communities over recent days amid allegations that Alaskan fishermen took more than double their normal catch of salmon so far this year.
"We're hopeful it will be able to go soon, but we just don't know," said Murray Sheppard, an official with the ferry line in Prince Rupert.

Despite expectations they would break the blockade on Monday, Canadian police said they were waiting for Alaska's representatives to serve the defiant fishermen with a court injunction compelling them to disperse.
Acting on a request by Alaska, a Canadian federal court on Sunday ordered the fishermen to release the ship.
"We haven't been given a timeframe..." for serving of the court order, said Mike Legault of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. "As of now, the group has grown to about 300 vessels."
Dissatisfied with Canada's handling of the situation, the United States on Monday told Canada to enforce the order.
"The United States has protested and continues to protest this blockade," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "...Canada must take action to enforce the court's judgment."

John Cummins, a Canadian member of parliament who is monitoring the situation, said the fishermen might soon free the ferry voluntarily. But they wanted assurances that Alaska will not seek financial damages from the protesters.

Canadian Fisheries Minister David Anderson showed no sign of trying to intervene in the blockade when he arrived in Prince Rupert on Monday. He was due to fly over the fishing grounds before meeting with fishermen Monday night.
"I am not here to lift the blockade," he told reporters. "I am here ... to meet with the fishermen and discuss their concerns."
In Vancouver, British Columbia Premier Glen Clark released an open letter he had sent to U.S. President Bill Clinton, calling Alaska's fishing "piracy" and urging him to intervene.

The flotilla of fishing boats first prevented the ferry from sailing on Saturday after it made a regular stop in Prince Rupert on its way from Seattle to Ketchikan, Alaska. Irate fishermen shouted obscenities and burned an American flag, Canadian media reported.

The current tensions follow years of squabbling over salmon. Canada last week accused the United States of violating a treaty between the two countries by overfishing in Alaska, but the United States rejected the claim. Canada wants the two countries to submit the dispute to binding international arbitration.
